newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Tribal clashes in Indonesia's Irian Jaya continue.
newsitem.headline: Tribal clashes in Indonesia's Irian Jaya continue.

text.p: Tribal clashes around the mining town of Timika in Indonesia's remote Irian Jaya province continued on Saturday as residents said the death toll from the fighting had risen to five.

"The disturbances have continued again today. They haven't really stopped since they began on Thursday. There's hundreds of people involved," one resident in Timika, some 4,000 km (2,500 miles) east of Jakarta, told Reuters by telephone.

The fighting between mostly Amungme and Dani tribesmen had its origins in a fight late on Wednesday between small groups of men from both tribes in a village in the Kwamki Lama district, about five km (three miles) north of Timika, residents said.
It was triggered by a robbery or extortion attempt, they said.

Early on Thursday, Amungme men made a revenge attack, burning houses of rival Dani people, escalating the dispute into a small-scale tribal war fought with traditional weapons including axes, spears, arrows and clubs.
The resident said five people had died since the fighting started, although another reliable sources in the town said four had been confirmed dead on Thursday.

However, the source said that 14 had been injured in the fighting on Friday and two of these were critically injured and not expected to live. The same source added 15 were injured on Thursday. Police have confirmed only two deaths.
"There was a little bit of fighting this morning, but there were no victims," a policeman in Timika said on Saturday, declining to give any further details.

Residents said a traditional peace ceremony or pig roast scheduled for Saturday in the highlands involving both tribes, meant to smooth the rift after another tribal war in the area in January, had been indefinitely postponed.
"It could not go ahead because of the new fighting. It's been cancelled for the time being," one Amungme resident said.
In January, six people were killed and more than 60 injured when thousands of Amungme and Dani tribesman clashed near Tembagapura after an alleged rape.

PT Freeport Indonesia, operator of one of the world's largest copper and gold mines at Tembagapura, about 45 km (28 miles) north of Timika, is 81.28 percent owned by Freeport McMoRan Copper and Gold Inc of the United States. Indonesian interests own the balance.
Company officials have said the relatively isolated lowlands clash has not affected operations at the high-altitude mine.

Indonesia, the world's most populous Moslem nation, has been beset by a series of ethnic and religious clashes in recent months in West Kalimantan province on Borneo island and the main island of Java.
